awd_titl_txt: I-Corps: Translation Potential of a Novel Drug Discovery Platform for Targeting G-protein-coupled Receptor Sites
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader impact/commercial potential of this I-Corps project is based on the development of a platform that enables the discovery of highly specific drugs targeting a unique site on G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs). GPCRs are a large family of cell surface receptors that play a crucial role in transmitting signals from the outside to the inside of cells. These receptors are among the most important drug targets in modern medicine, with many medications, including beta-blockers, antihistamines, and psychiatric drugs, interacting with specific GPCRs. Nearly one-third of all FDA-approved drugs target GPCRs, representing approximately 30% ($890 billion) of the global pharmaceutical market share.  GPCRs are desirable drug targets for two main reasons: their druggable sites are easily accessible, and they directly regulate a wide range of physiological and disease processes. However, conventional GPCR-targeted drugs face limitations in terms of safety and efficacy, restricting the patient populations they can effectively treat. This project proposes a novel drug discovery platform targeting this new GCPR druggable site that could overcome these limitations, enabling the identification of new drug candidates and the development of more effective, safer, and innovative therapies more rapidly.

This I-Corps project utilizes experiential learning coupled with first-hand investigation of the industry ecosystem to assess the translation potential of the proposed technology. It is based on the prior development of a platform technology that enables drug discovery related activities specific to a new molecular mechanism of action targeting G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) as a new druggable site. Compared to other druggable sites on GPCRs, this site is highly specific in terms of its composition among the 800+ different receptor isoforms. The technology that was developed in the process of characterizing this new site is a platform that enables identification of compounds that target this site. A key component of this platform is a patented high-throughput screening assay that detects nuanced differences in GPCR drug effectiveness that are not detectable using other high-throughput screening formats.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Our team entered the I-Corps program with the idea of a platform technology for the development of more effective therapeutics with lower side effect burdens. Through the award period, our team conducted a total of 113 customer discovery interviews across the drug discovery business ecosystem, with stakeholders in three main areas: therapeutics discovery, pre-clinical development, and clinical deployment.

Our first key learning through our customer discovery interviews was that a platform technology for drug discovery, on its own, does not make for a compelling business case. We learned that we needed to apply our technology to one singular therapeutics opportunity that presents the quickest path to a proof of concept.

Through our interviews, we learned that weight management therapeutics would be the best therapeutic area to focus our technology development on. This is a highly competitive area in early-stage drug discovery, presenting a challenging environment to differentiate our approach from other emerging therapeutic approaches. We originally thought that the potential of our approach to decrease GI side effects compared to the current standard-of-care would be the key value proposition for our technology in the obesity space. However, our customer discovery interviews invalidated this value proposition. Instead, we learned that an emerging unmet need in the obesity therapeutics space is the ability for a drug regiment to “bias” fat loss over muscle loss.

We worked diligently to generate a proof-of-concept for out technology to demonstrate this unmet need, generating a prototype “tool” biologic that promotes lipid metabolism in an in vitro model system of adipose tissue. This proof-of-concept data has been critical for our most recent interviews with potential customers in early-stage drug discovery for obesity therapeutics. While these interviews identified potential risks in further developing our biologic into a therapeutic, there was excitement for our platform technology to more broadly address side effect burden and therapeutic efficacy.

As a follow-up to these more recent interviews, we are discussing pilot projects with two different biopharmaceutical companies to use our technology to generate tool biologics. If successful, we would out-license these research tools back to the biopharmaceutical companies. Professor Sivaramakrishnan (Technical Lead and PI) and Dr. Sadler (Entrepreneurial Lead) are actively involved in launching these pilot projects at the University of Minnesota.

Our larger goal, however, is to pursue our own commercialization of our technology in the form of a start-up company, Oxbow Therapeutics. Mitigating the technical risk of our tool biologics, as identified in our more recent customer discovery interviews, aligns well with some of the broader research goals of Prof. Sivaramakrishnan’s laboratory. Professor Sivaramakrishnan and Dr. Sadler are also actively pursuing this line of scientific inquiry. They are still engaged with their industry mentor, Dr. Mark Robbins, for strategy involving out-licensing technologies from the University of Minnesota and pursuing investment. While it is still the beginning of the journey for the Oxbow Therapeutics team, our training in the I-Corps program has pointed us in a direction in which we can confidently venture.
